papers.title: An Exploration of Attacks on AI Agent Systems
papers.abstract: As autonomous AI agents become more integrated into sensitive domains, it is crucial that single and multi-agent AI systems are secured. This paper investigates how prompt injection attacks can exploit both direct user inputs and inter?agent communication to leak sensitive information and trigger cross-agent infections. While our tests mostly highlight key vulnerabilities in single-agent systems, we also extend these attacks to multi-agent frameworks, investigating how weaknesses can propagate across agents. Our findings emphasize the need for more robust defenses as AI agents become more commonly embedded in real-world workflows.

papers.title: SoK: Privacy-Preserving Order Matching
papers.abstract: Privacy-preserving order matching enables traders to discover and execute compatible orders while limiting disclosure of sensitive trading information. Existing systems span financial markets and blockchain-based asset exchanges and employ diverse market structures, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions, making their privacy guarantees difficult to compare. We present a systematization of privacy-preserving order matching covering 22 protocol families. We organize the order lifecycle into four phases: order representation and submission, order discovery and collection, order-matching, and settlement, and characterize each phase by protected and exposed information, access roles, privacy mechanisms, and trust assumptions. Our analysis shows that privacy is not a single protocol-level property: protecting selected order attributes or individual phases does not necessarily prevent leakage elsewhere in the lifecycle. We identify recurring trade-offs among privacy, functionality, trust, and verifiability, highlighting the challenge of achieving end-to-end privacy across the complete order lifecycle.

papers.title: Organizational Context for the Enterprise Security Brain
papers.abstract: Agents that investigate and decide on enterprise security reason over a machine-readable view of the environment: its assets, identities, configurations, relations, and findings. The correct judgment about an asset also depends on what the organization knows about it: who owns it, what business function it serves, which policy governs it, and which risks were accepted. Part of this knowledge can be inferred from machine state, such as an ownership tag; most of it is recorded by people in policies, audit reports, architecture diagrams, tickets, and conversations, outside machine state. We call this distance the organizational context gap. Closing it poses four challenges: extracting the right claims from heterogeneous organizational data and, at inference time, detecting claims made stale by live state, checking live state against the governing policy, and binding architecture diagrams, which carry the business logic, to live resources. We introduce organizational context as a layer of the enterprise security brain and define it with a taxonomy and six properties its representation must preserve. We then define a context model in which a claim carries one meaning, an attestation records each source that asserts it, strength is derived from live evidence at read time, and claims resolve onto the entities of the asset graph. On a production environment spanning AWS, Okta, Google Workspace, and GitHub, extraction recovers 0.80 of a pooled 1,355-claim ground truth at 0.87 precision, with 0.5% of extracted claims unsupported by their source. An agent reasoning over live state and resolved context raises the conflict in 0.97 of stale-finding tasks, and reaches answer correctness of 0.83 on policy-alignment tasks and 0.86 on architecture tasks.

papers.title: HOMARD: Hammering Off-chip Memory via Aggregate power Rail Disclosure
papers.abstract: Software-based microarchitectural attacks have mainly exploited timing differences to infer information from DRAM. However, defenses and optimizations can prevent timing-based approaches from resolving precise microarchitectural behaviors. We show that unprivileged millisecond- and milliampere-resolution power sensors on modern Arm SoCs can recover DRAM mapping functions and reveal the data dependence of memory accesses without timers. We present HOMARD, a methodology that reads DRAM activity from this telemetry, and two attack primitives. HOMARD-RE is a hierarchy-aware linear-algebraic method that reverse-engineers DRAM addressing functions from power alone. HOMARD-DATA recovers the Hamming weight of a fetched cache line through joint-power rail templating and secret byte values through correlation power analysis on the same rails. Across an AMD ZCU102, a Raspberry Pi 5, and a multi-chip-based LPDDR4 NVIDIA Jetson TX2, HOMARD-RE succeeds where row-buffer timing methods fail. On the Pi 5, HOMARD-DATA classifies 9 Hamming-weight levels at 81.5% accuracy and recovers secret bytes in minutes by correlating rail current with data-dependent bit toggling between neighbors in a row. Both primitives work with an architectural load or a mispredicted Spectre-RSB path on which no value is architecturally read. These results establish unprivileged power telemetry as an independent side channel for profiled microarchitectural attacks, particularly when timing falls silent.

papers.title: Cancerous Backdoor Attack: Gradual Activation via Invisible Tokens and A Stage Controller
papers.abstract: Backdoor Attacks on Large Language Models (LLMs) typically follow a trigger-response pattern, where satisfying a trigger condition activates a single terminal behavior. However, this single-point backdoor activation does not explore attacks in which malicious behavior develops gradually through multiple intermediate stages before reaching the terminal activation stage. We present Cancerous Backdoor Attack, that gradually corrupts an LLM's reasoning over a sequence of interactions by leveraging invisible tokens and a stage controller. Specifically, invisible tokens provide hidden stages to the model without appearing in the user's visible request and the stage controller tracks the attack's progression during inference to realize gradual activation. We evaluate Cancerous Backdoor Attack across several reasoning datasets. The attack consistently produces gradual reasoning corruption across models and tasks. We compare Cancerous Backdoor Attack with prior backdoor attack baselines to demonstrate our proposed attack outperforms the baselines. Our results indicate that reasoning corruption can develop gradually before it becomes visible, making answer accuracy alone insufficient for detecting backdoor attacks.

papers.title: Enabling Extended SGX Enclaves inside Confidential Virtual Machines
papers.abstract: Confidential Virtual Machines (CVMs), such as AMD SEV-SNP, and process enclaves, such as Intel SGX, provide workload protection against cloud threats. However, they strongly differ in TCB, deployment cost and speed, peer workload protection, resource sharing, fine-grained isolation and attestation, and programming capabilities. Nesting process enclaves within CVMs offers an optimal solution and an opportunity to address long-standing SGX limitations: lack of intra-enclave protection, expensive transitions and exception paths, slow enclave cloning, and a restricted programming model that limits Library Operating Systems (LibOS). This paper introduces TEEVisor, a CVM-resident architecture consisting of a security monitor and a kernel driver that leverages AMD SEV-SNP Virtual Machine Privilege Levels (VMPLs) to build hardware-protected, process-level enclaves inside a guest CVM with two modes: (1) an SGX binary compatibility mode to run unmodified SGX applications; and (2) a novel extended SGX~(eSGX) mode optimizing slow execution paths and offering richer enclave programming capabilities. On commercial AMD EPYC hardware, against native CVM execution, TEEVisor incurs under 5% overhead on compute- and memory-bound workloads, around 12% on I/O-heavy applications, and accelerates enclave cloning to a rate of 93~$\mu$s/MB of enclave size, demonstrating that eSGX semantics inside a CVM are practical for production use.

papers.title: PVBRF-ID: Private, Verifiable and Byzantine-Robust Federated Intrusion Detection for Oilfield Enterprise Networks
papers.abstract: Federated learning allows dispersed oilfield sites to train a shared intrusion detector without pooling network traffic, yet its aggregation step forces a choice between privacy and robustness. Byzantine-robust rules must read each update in the clear, whereas secure aggregation hides updates from the checks that detect poisoning. We present PVBRF-ID, a two-server protocol in which sites secret-share their updates and the servers jointly test each update's norm and its cosine similarity to a reference computed on a small clean root set, revealing one accept bit per site. Commitments, Merkle roots and a homomorphic audit make the inclusion of accepted updates publicly verifiable. On a 15-class Edge-IIoTset task with ten sites holding differently distributed data and ten random seeds, PVBRF-ID matched FedAvg on clean data (macro-F1 0.708 vs. 0.706) and withstood sign-flip attacks (0.696 vs. 0.091). Against an adaptive attacker controlling 30% of sites, PVBRF-ID with secure clipping reached 0.641, whereas FedAvg fell to 0.046; plaintext multi-Krum remained higher by 0.052. An update-inference attacker recovered each site's class mix from plaintext updates (Spearman correlation 0.81) but not from one server's view. Backdoors passed the filter, and noise-based mitigation gave only heuristic protection. The implementation uses Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3, 30 rounds and 10 seeds.

papers.title: Better Batches, Better Privacy: Random Allocation for DP-BandMF
papers.abstract: The current state of the art for batch selection and noise addition in differentially private training is a combination of DP-BandMF (informally, DP-SGD where the noise added in two different steps can be correlated if the steps are within $b$ of each other) and privacy amplification by sampling via Monte Carlo accounting. First, whereas prior batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF were inspired by Poisson sampling, random allocation is known to outperform Poisson sampling for DP-SGD. We therefore propose and analyze new batch selection strategies for DP-BandMF inspired by random allocation, improving RMSE by up to $1.85\times$ over previous work. Second, Monte Carlo accounting typically requires drawing $\Omega(1/\delta)$ samples from a privacy loss distribution, making accounting costly. We increase sampling and scoring throughput by two orders of magnitude through a carefully optimized GPU implementation. Finally, previous work chose the DP-BandMF strategy matrix and the batch selection strategy independently. We give a simple framework for choosing these parameters jointly, reducing RMSE by up to $13.4\%$ over fixed strategy matrices.

papers.title: Onions in the ATmosphere: Decentralizing Trust in Identity
papers.abstract: Multiple approaches have been implemented for identities that associate meaningful identifiers, such as domain names, with self-authenticating identifiers, such as onion addresses. While these approaches offer various advantages both from identifier meaningfulness and from identifier self-authentication, identifier association itself is subject to blocking, hijack, fingerprinting, and other forms of surveillance and manipulation. So too are the resources associated with an identity comprising a meaningful identifier and a self-authenticating identifier. This paper describes ongoing work on two such approaches to self-authenticating meaningful identity (SAMI): associating a registered domain name with an onion address (onion association) and associating an atproto handle with a decentralized identifier (DID association). We present both the application of already implemented and published means of secure onion association to DID association and the combination of both in a single identity. Finally, we describe grounding identity association and integrity in contextual trust, wherein trusting attestations of identity relies on contextual relevance of an attestor to the identity rather than relying only on structural authority, for example as embodied in the traditional centralized infrastructure.

papers.title: Power, Performance, and Area of HPC-Based Malware Detectors: An FPGA and Open-PDK ASIC Study
papers.abstract: Hardware malware detectors (HMDs) classify programs as benign or malicious based on hardware performance counter (HPC) data. Previous studies have shown that ensemble classifiers outperform other classifiers on detection metrics. However, the area, power, and timing costs of HMDs remain open questions. We address these questions across a comprehensive design space comprising multiple classifier families, variable HPC sets, and ensemble learning methods. We designed a pipeline to reconstruct selected trained models, generate synthesizable register-transfer-level (RTL) implementations, validate each design against a bit-accurate golden model, and evaluate the implementations. The results show that tree- and rule-based detectors achieve the highest detection performance with nearly an order of magnitude less area and several times lower energy than function-based classifiers. Reducing the number of HPC inputs to fit a processor's concurrent-counter limit preserves detection performance while substantially reducing area, power, and delay.

papers.title: VEPA: Verified Evolving Formal Policy for Lifelong LLM Agent Guardrails
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly operate over sensitive resources, such as private documents and mutable system states, which can create serious safety and security risks. Runtime guardrails should therefore make inspectable, reproducible, and deterministic allow or refuse decisions before potentially irreversible agent actions are executed. However, safety and security requirements are rarely complete before deployment, so guardrails need to keep adapting as new risks emerge. Existing adaptive guardrails learn from deployment experience, but they usually apply safety policies through LLM inference, which can lead to inconsistent decisions and ambiguous policy interpretations. Formal guardrails, on the other hand, enforce policies deterministically, but they usually rely on pre-deployment or task-specific policies and have no mechanism to adapt to newly observed risks. We introduce VEPA, a framework for the verified evolution of formal agent guardrails. VEPA represents the guardrail as a formal policy of executable symbolic rules over typed agent events. During deployment, we use an LLM guided by deployment feedback to propose policy patches that fix newly observed failures while preserving previously correct behavior. Then, a deterministic verifier only accepts policies that are structurally valid and conflict-free. Finally, an evidence-aware authority layer activates a verified rule only when it has enough supporting evidence, so uncertain updates cannot directly affect guardrail decisions. Across ASSEBench-Safety, ASSEBench-Security, and ATBench, VEPA consistently outperforms baselines while expanding the scope of deterministic formal-policy enforcement. These gains also hold under more challenging deployment conditions, including mixed streams, corrupted feedback, and longer horizons.

papers.title: Reward Hacking as a Transmissible Strategy in Multi-Agent Coding Systems
papers.abstract: Multi-agent systems are increasingly used to solve coding tasks by coordinating agents that share code and plans. These agents are often optimized with reinforcement learning (RL) using automated evaluators, but bypassing evaluation can earn reward without producing a genuine solution. Prior work has largely treated reward hacking as a single-agent failure. In this work, we show that a reward-hacking strategy elicited in one agent can propagate to others and affect system coordination. Across four open-weight backbones, coding RL elicits and amplifies reward hacking in two settings: explicit mechanism descriptions in the system prompt and mid-training that models upstream exposure to facts about the coding environment. Using post-RL agents from the mid-training setting as sources, we observe propagation through code and shared memory, and across roles through natural-language plans. Even agents based on small open-weight models induce reward hacking in stronger closed-weight targets. On hard tasks, propagation can intensify along a transmission chain after the original source leaves as the code acquires more persuasive justifications. We also theoretically analyze conditions under which reward hacking amplifies, persists, or decays across agent interactions. Beyond propagation, reward hacking can bias task routing toward reward-hacking agents and survive candidate aggregation. As potential mitigations, we evaluate code review by the coder or a separate verifier, both of which reduce delivered hacks. Together, these results establish reward hacking as a transmissible strategy whose effects extend beyond the agent in which it first emerges.

papers.title: Vulnerable Models in the AI Supply Chain: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Propagation, and Usage Patterns
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has established a complex supply chain, but many of these shared artifacts harbor severe vulnerabilities such as insecure serialization and architectural backdoors. While prior efforts have extensively scanned model registries to flag malicious artifacts, a critical gap remains in understanding how developers actually adopt and integrate these unsafe models into downstream software systems. We bridge this gap by conducting a large-scale empirical study on the usage and propagation of 16,977 known vulnerable models on HuggingFace flagged by InsightDB. We track their prevalence across GitHub repositories, software packages, fine-tuning chains, and deployed applications. Our analysis reveals that, despite being publicly flagged, these vulnerable models appear in over 21,000 code locations across more than 5,000 open-source repositories, with 3,757 distinct flagged models (22.1\%) actively referenced in at least one project. To understand how these models are integrated in code and identify recurring usage patterns, we categorize and analyze the recurring patterns surrounding them via a customized pipeline that combines Code Property Graphs extraction with a tailored Frequent Subgraph Mining approach. Across all patterns, we find no evidence of provenance verification or model sanitization logic, with developers frequently bypassing security parameters or delegating trust to permissive framework defaults. These findings underscore that scanning model files alone is insufficient, highlighting the urgent need for context-aware security analysis and stricter integration guardrails at the application layer of the AI supply chain.

papers.title: Sample-Preserving Search-to-Decision Reduction for Noisy Linear Equations over Large Moduli
papers.abstract: The Noisy Linear Equations problem involves finding the solution to a random linear system over a finite field given noisy evaluations. This is a generalisation of various learning problems widely used in cryptography, including Learning with Errors (LWE), Learning with Rounding (LWR), and Learning Parity with Noise (LPN). We present a new sample-preserving search-to-decision reduction for Noisy Linear Equations that has complexity $\mathrm{poly}(n,m,\log q, q/\sigma)$, where $n$ is the dimension of the secret, $m$ is the number of samples, $q$ is the modulus, and $\sigma$ is the magnitude of the noise (defined suitably for the kind of noise involved). In particular, this implies search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR that run in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)$ even if the modulus $q$ is exponentially large, as long as the noise-to-modulus ratio $\sigma/q$ is non-negligible. Our reduction works for prime moduli $q$. If $q$ is composite, it instead produces a list that contains a small multiple of the solution. Prior to this work, known search-to-decision reductions for LWE and LWR either did not preserve the parameters of the problem (i.e., $m$, $n$, $\sigma$, and $q$), or had complexity that scaled polynomially with either $\sigma$ or the largest prime factor of $q$.

papers.title: AgentValve: Sybil-Resilient Payment Authorization for Permissionless AI Markets
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it using six months of Ethereum data and synthetic workloads. Experimental results show that under attacks with up to 10,000 synthetic Sybil identities and with chosen attackers, the payment exposure and capacity depletion remain bounded. Regarding practicality, the witness-commit mechanism lowers admission cost by up to 40.8% compared with baselines, and admitting common payments costs approximately \$0.04-\$0.21.

papers.title: WaveMark: Robust Wavelet-Domain Image Watermarking for Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Image watermarking enables provenance tracing for photorealistic images generated by diffusion models. However, state-of-the-art (SOTA) removal attacks can suppress embedded signals with little perceptual degradation. This vulnerability limits the effectiveness of watermarks for intellectual property protection and misuse attribution. We propose WaveMark, a novel wavelet-domain watermarking method that embeds messages in a diffusion model's initial noise. To support robust recovery from perturbed carriers, WaveMark distributes keyed replicas of message bits across spatial positions, wavelet orientations, and scales. Each carrier groups coefficients from four latent channels and encodes a randomized bit through magnitude projection, providing an explicit decoding margin. We evaluate WaveMark with SD2.1 on SDP and MS-COCO Captions under 14 attacks. WaveMark achieves 100.0% bit accuracy (BA) without attacks, while maintaining image quality comparable to the evaluated baselines. Under SOTA MarkNull and MarkNull-A, it retains over 88% BA, outperforming all baselines.

papers.title: Post-Quantum Session Establishment for Matter over Thread: Message Size, Transport, and Protocol Options
papers.abstract: Matter's first post-quantum change protects device attestation with ML-DSA, but its operational handshake, CASE, still derives session keys from P-256 ECDH, so recorded traffic can be decrypted once a quantum computer exists. We quantify the cost of moving CASE to ML-KEM and post-quantum signatures over Thread, where frames carry at most 127 bytes and a Matter message at most 1178 bytes. A byte-exact model of the CASE messages shows that a drop-in ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-44 handshake grows from 1.6 kB to 22.8 kB and that no fully post-quantum configuration built from FIPS 203/204/205 algorithms fits the message limit. A Monte Carlo model of multi-hop Thread, calibrated to OpenThread and Matter source constants, shows that sending these messages as fragmented IPv6 datagrams causes spurious retransmissions whenever a message and its reply outlast Matter's retransmission timer. At three to four hops the drop-in handshake then takes 1.8 to 2.6 times longer than with a selective-repeat block transfer, with or without interference, and up to 33% of handshakes with sleepy devices fail; raising the timers does not remove the effect. Caching certificate chains and authenticating the device with a pre-distributed ML-KEM key reduce the handshake to 6.1 kB and 44 ms of device computation. As a first step, hybrid P-256+ML-KEM-512 key exchange with a cached device chain protects session keys against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks while every message still fits the current limit.

papers.title: Provably Subexponential Algorithms for Bounded-Error LWE with Few Samples
papers.abstract: We show that a variant of the Wagner/BKW-style algorithm for LWE of Kirchner and Fouque [KF15] solves decision and search LWE with secrets of size $n$ over prime moduli $q=n^{\kappa+o(1)}$, for any fixed $\kappa>0$, with errors bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, in time $2^{O(n/\ln\ln n)}$ given $n+O(n/\ln\ln n)$ original samples. Further, if each coordinate of the secret is also bounded by $\exp((\ln n)^{o(1)})$, the same time bound holds with errors bounded by $n^{o(1)}$ and only $O(n/\ln\ln q)$ samples. Earlier, it was known that Kirchner and Fouque's algorithm could solve LWE with these parameters in subexponential time with a much larger number of samples $m = \Omega(n\log{n})$ [HKM18]. Ducas et al. [DEL25] showed that an adaptation of this algorithm could solve the corresponding dual, the $\mathrm{SIS}^{\infty}$ problem, with a suitable norm bound $q/\operatorname{polylog}(n)$ and $m=n+\omega(n/\ln\ln n)$ variables in subexponential time. Whereas their analysis involves interpreting the algorithm in terms of chains of lattices, our approach is quite elementary and is based on bounding the lower moments of a Fourier statistic.

papers.title: Space Over Statistic, Retraining Over Ranking: Auditing Training Labels Under Label-Only Backdoors
papers.abstract: Some backdoor attacks never touch an image. FLIP only changes labels: on CIFAR-10, flipping 3% of them makes a ResNet-32 send 99.7% of triggered source-class images to the attacker's class. The usual defenses look for the poison inside a model trained on those same labels. So when they struggle, is the problem the test they run, or the space they run it in? We answer with a controlled swap: we keep the test, the labels and the metric fixed, change only the feature space, and judge each defense by retraining the victim on what it keeps. The space decides. On dog$\to$cat the same nearest-neighbor check scores AUROC 0.546 on the poisoned model's features, 0.967 on frozen DINOv2 features that never saw a label, and 0.995 on the same network trained on clean labels, an oracle control rather than a defense. We reproduce SPECTRE, the defense FLIP's authors recommend, to 90.94 / 0.97 against its published 91.47 / 1.7, then price it: on truck$\to$deer it deletes 20% of every class, while a prototype audit on the frozen features deletes 6% for higher clean accuracy and lower attack success. On three harder pairs that audit leaves about a quarter of the attack standing. A count read off encoder geometry and clean labels, before any attack is run, separates the pair where the audit removes the attack from those where it only partly does, though on a single zero-count pair. Three results warn against the easy story. A better detection score does not mean a safer model: on two of four pairs Confident Learning scores the higher AUROC, and on dog$\to$cat leaves 2.6 times the attack success. The prototype family, our best static performer, is the first an adaptive attacker slips past. And past a point, catching more poisons stops reducing attack success. Check labels in a space that never learned them, and judge a defense by the retrained model, not by its detection score.

papers.title: CAPE - Context-Aware Prioritization Engine for Vulnerability Scoring and Management
papers.abstract: Vulnerability patching is critical for safeguarding an enterprise's software ecosystem from cyber attacks. However, patching requires adequate preparation for potential system downtime and for unforeseen effects of the patched software on a live system. Thus, effective risk mitigation requires prioritization strategies that explicitly account for the operational context of the affected software. While vulnerability prioritization based on Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS), Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) and CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, can help, their differing goals and methodologies often lead to inconsistent, context-unaware decisions resulting in mis-allocated remediation efforts. In this work, we present the Context-Aware Prioritization Engine (CAPE), a vulnerability analysis framework that enriches each vulnerability scanner report of vulnerabilities (CVEs) with deployment-specific evidence. This evidence is used to perform vulnerability reachability, centrality, and exploitability analysis, producing a ranked priority score for the effective distribution of remediation effort. We evaluate CAPE on 30 open-source agentic applications comprising 6,138 scanner-reported CVEs. Our evaluation shows that a significant majority of CVEs are not reachable and exploitable which results in significant disparities between CAPE and context-free baselines - the CVSS, EPSS, and KEV. It also shows that CAPE consistently surfaces confirmed-exploitable CVEs at higher priority than all baselines, demonstrating that context-aware analysis provides substantially more accurate remediation guidance than context-free severity scoring alone.

papers.title: The Limits of Query Monitoring against Distributed Model Extraction
papers.abstract: Model providers now face distillation campaigns run through thousands of accounts, each of which looks like an ordinary user. When network and payment metadata cannot link those accounts, the only evidence left is what they ask. We study what a provider can and cannot learn from those queries alone, using one million real chat turns for development and 17 later weeks that no design choice touched for a single frozen evaluation. The answer is set less by anything specific to extraction than by benign coordination: a campaign is visible only if it is more distinctive than the most distinctive group of ordinary users in the same week. We make this precise, show that a small but positive difference between campaign and users buys a detection time rather than detectability, and identify the campaign that is hardest to detect. Empirically, a calibrated monitor catches naive distributed extraction that per-account monitors miss (0.86-1.00 of weeks), and one variant - selecting accounts that move together after discounting how topical each one is - still catches campaigns padded with natural text (0.50-0.96 of weeks) where the other two spectral detectors catch none. Distilling each campaign into a small student shows that, in our testbed, campaigns that evaded every detector kept at most 42% of the capability of a detectable one. The limits are equally concrete: a campaign that ramps up slowly poisons every detector's calibration, benign evaluation pipelines look exactly like distillation, we found no deployable detector at colluder shares of 2.5% or below, and campaigns that relay real users' requests may be invisible to any query-only monitor.

papers.title: Safety Graph: When Safety Responses Become Attack Surfaces in Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: Modern industrial control systems (ICS) are susceptible to cyber attacks triggering safety failures in the operational technology (OT) layer. The traditional way to mitigate any failure in OT is to implement safety responses. However, we show in this work that these responses can open up new attack surfaces, thereby vastly expanding the scope of lateral movement. Existing frameworks model cyber-to-physical escalation but provide no mechanism to reason about how these safety responses to OT-failures can trigger new cascading cyber attacks in the Information Technology (IT) layer. To enable such reasoning, we introduce Safety Graph (SG), a formal framework unifying three paradigms - Attack Graphs (AG), Fault Trees (FT), and Event Trees (ET) - over a shared propositional state space, capturing the full bidirectional IT-OT cascade. We provide a sound and complete compilation of SG to a classical AI planning problem, performing plan search using A* to find cross-layer cascade paths. Through a Web3D modeling and simulation of the Tennessee Eastman chemical process plant, which is a widely used chemical engineering benchmark serving as a standard for testing control, monitoring and fault propagation, we demonstrate that the planning compilation of SG automatically discovers safety-response-induced lateral movements, and identifies the responsible barriers that are unidentifiable under existing models. A complexity and scalability analysis characterizes how the planning compilation of SG scales with model size and cascade depth. To the best of our knowledge, SG is the first framework to formally model IT-OT attacks and enable operators to explore the problem of cyber attacks triggering cascading failures in ICS.

papers.title: Understanding Verification Vulnerabilities in Cross-chain Bridges: An Empirical Study
authors: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
Jiachi Chen (The State Key Laboratory of Blockchain
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.abstract: With the rapid development of blockchain technology, numerous heterogeneous blockchains have emerged, each featuring distinct architectures, consensus mechanisms, and application ecosystems. Cross-chain bridges have consequently become a critical infrastructure component, typically relying on smart contracts to facilitate message passing and asset transfers across heterogeneous blockchains. Unlike single-chain contracts, bridge contracts introduce additional verification logic to validate external-chain data, such as state proofs, message sender identities, and signatures. However, correctly implementing such logic is challenging. We refer to vulnerabilities that violate the security guarantees of cross-chain verification as Cross-chain Verification Vulnerabilities (CVVs). To characterize CVVs, we conduct the first systematic empirical study of this vulnerability class. By analyzing 588 security audit reports from 36 real-world cross-chain bridge projects, we derive 11 CVV patterns and organize them into 5 high-level categories according to the affected verification properties. Following this taxonomy, we construct a CVV dataset containing 830 vulnerability instances across 786 contract files. The dataset establishes mappings among audit reports, audited source-code versions, affected source files, and CVV-pattern labels. We then assess existing detection approaches. Current tools provide limited documented coverage of CVV patterns, while only two of four evaluated LLMs outperform an all-pattern constant baseline of 29.3% Macro-F1; the best reaches 51.2%. Together, the limited tool coverage and inconsistent LLM gains motivate detection methods tailored to cross-chain verification semantics.

papers.title: Understanding and Mitigating Cross-Session Attacks via Persistent Artifacts in Agent Skill Composition
papers.abstract: Agent skills extend the capabilities of AI agents by bundling instructions, code, and resources into reusable packages. During skill execution, agents may produce or modify artifacts, such as files, configurations, and cached data, that are reused by other skills in later sessions. Since these artifacts can persist across sessions and later be accessed by other skills, they introduce a new attack surface that can be exploited to influence subsequent executions. However, the security risks arising from such cross-session skill interactions remain largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate cross-session composition attacks in skill-based AI agents and develop a runtime defense against them. Specifically, we characterize three attack mechanisms, namely Instruction Propagation (IP), Data Boundary Violation (DBV), and Evidence Poisoning (EP), through which malicious effects propagate across skill executions via persistent artifacts. To evaluate whether existing agents can resist these attacks while completing legitimate tasks, we construct SkillRelayBench, a benchmark of 270 adversarial cases drawn from 30 cross-session skill-composition scenarios across ten domains. Our evaluation of seven models across Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, and Claude Code reveals attack success rates (ASR) ranging from 46.7% to 77.4% and attack chain success rates (ACSR) ranging from 35.6% to 61.1%. Successful attack chains cover all five target security consequence categories, highlighting the broad impact of these attacks. To mitigate these risks, we propose SkillRelayGuard, which restores artifact provenance context and provides pre-execution advisory review while leaving the final execution decision to the agent. Evaluation across three agent settings shows that SkillRelayGuard reduces overall ASR from 69.5% to 10.9% and ACSR from 54.8% to 10.0%, while increasing legitimate task completion from 79.6% to 87.5%.

papers.title: Quantization-Tolerant Gradient Auditing for Active Inference-Attack Detection in Federated Learning
papers.abstract: Inside a federated learning system a participant can quietly study the shared model and learn about others' private data. The usual defense, differential privacy, often adds so much noise that the model is no longer worth training. In cross-silo FL, where participants are a few accountable organizations and the server is trusted, we ask whether the server can instead interrogate clients. Each round it sends a secret challenge batch and asks every client to return a checksum of the gradient that batch induces, together with a timing. A client that mutated the model state, as an active generative-adversarial-network discriminator attacker does, returns a wrong checksum. We make this checksum robust to benign cross-platform floating-point non-determinism with a quantized fingerprint compared under a small tolerance. It flags two distinct active attacks at a true-positive rate of $1.0$ with no false positives on the checksum axis, stable across the fingerprint's parameters and up to $50$ clients at malicious ratios to $40\%$, for $32\,\mathrm{ms}$ of server work and $4.35\,\mathrm{kB}$ per response. Against a purely passive attacker the only signal is timing, and it is not robust: a cohort-relative test detects only in low-jitter conditions while a false-positive-free per-client baseline is blind, so no configuration delivers both. An attacker that answers the challenge on an untouched copy of the model while tampering with a replica evades the audit entirely. Therefore the checksum is a reliable in-band signal against attackers that do not decouple the audited computation from the attacked one, and it composes with differential privacy, whose accuracy cost we quantify on Texas100, rather than replacing it.

papers.title: LETHE: Defending against Unauthorized Image-to-Video Generation via Value Diversity Collapse
papers.abstract: Image-to-video (I2V) diffusion models can animate a single reference image into high-quality, subject-consistent videos, posing threats of misuse as anyone can turn personal photos into fabricated videos without consent. A promising solution is to proactively add an adversarial perturbation to the image before release, such that videos generated from it would be unfaithful or visually corrupted. However, due to an insufficient understanding of what governs how subsequent frames read the reference image in modern I2V models, existing protections struggle to offer strong protection under common perturbation budgets. In this paper, we approach the problem by exploring this underlying reading mechanism. Through a convex geometric analysis, we theoretically identify the spread of the reference value vectors as a key factor governing this reading process, and empirically find that even a mild contraction of this spread can severely degrade the generated video, making it an efficient lever for protection. Guided by this insight, we propose LETHE, a novel protection method that directly disrupts this reading process. LETHE pairs two complementary objectives, where a value collapse objective drives the reference value vectors toward uniformity, while an attention attraction objective draws subsequent frames toward these collapsed tokens to amplify corruption. We further construct two human-centric I2V protection benchmarks and conduct extensive experiments with multiple modern I2V models, which demonstrate the state-of-the-art protection performance and versatility of LETHE.

papers.title: Secrets in Preamble: Practical and Robust PHY Information Hiding for Wi-Fi
papers.abstract: Physical layer (PHY) information hiding refers to the concealment of secrets within PHY waveforms without compromising the integrity of the primary communication link, thereby enabling critical applications such as covert communication, PHY steganography, and watermarking. The widespread deployment of Wi-Fi has motivated substantial research interest in hiding secrets within Wi-Fi waveforms. However, existing Wi-Fi information hiding approaches suffer from two limitations: restricted steganographic capacity and insufficient robustness against environmental variations, both of which severely constrain practical deployment. This work proposes to embed secrets within the Wi-Fi legacy short training field (L-STF). The designed method preserves the autocorrelation properties of Wi-Fi L-STF, ensuring that packet detection and coarse frequency offset compensation functionalities remain uncompromised. The secret embedding and extraction processes employ a pair of neural networks designed to learn optimal embedding rules and maximize steganographic capacity. We developed a prototype system and conducted comprehensive experiments across both indoor and outdoor environments. Experimental results show that our method can reliably embed 46 secret bits within Wi-Fi packets across diverse channel conditions, achieving significantly enhanced steganographic capacity and environmental robustness. The hardware prototype study validates the feasibility of the proposed Wi-Fi information hiding scheme.

papers.title: Towards Safe World Models: Risks, Defenses, and Evaluation
papers.abstract: World models support planning, control, learning from imagined experience, and model-mediated evaluation by predicting action-conditioned consequences. Their safety cannot be inferred from predictive accuracy alone: errors in observations, state and memory, dynamics, evaluation, execution, or feedback can propagate into unsafe decisions and persist through updates. This work organizes the literature on world-model safety around a six-stage lifecycle covering data and observations, state and memory, dynamics and imagination, evaluation and planning, action and control, and feedback and update. We synthesize non-adversarial failures, attacks, defenses, evaluation protocols, benchmarks, and deployment conditions, and distinguish evidence directness from outcome level. The current evidence corpus contains 163 cited works. We use the framework to identify where claims are supported, where attribution remains unresolved, and which measurements are needed to connect model-level behavior to closed-loop and operational safety.

papers.title: EviRepair: Evidence-Driven Agents for Reliable Vulnerability Repair
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled agent-based approaches for repository-level automated vulnerability repair (AVR), showing promising repair capabilities. However, an important issue has received limited attention: how can we ensure that the evidence generated during the repair process is reliable enough to support accurate vulnerability understanding and patch generation? In this paper, we propose EviRepair, an evidence-driven multi-agent framework for repository-level AVR. EviRepair introduces evidence review into the repair process by enabling agents to collaboratively collect vulnerability evidence, verify evidence consistency, and construct a reviewed vulnerability model for patch synthesis and validation. Extensive experiments on PatchEval and SecBench benchmarks with multiple agent frameworks and LLMs demonstrate that EviRepair consistently outperforms existing agent-based baselines, achieving average improvements of 16.37% and 40.33% in resolved rates on PatchEval and SecBench, respectively. Codes are available at https://github.com/lly-s/EviRepair

papers.title: A Systematic Study of Security Enforcement at Android Inter-Component Boundaries
papers.abstract: Android's inter-process communication (IPC) mechanisms (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers, ContentProviders, and URI scheme handlers) form the primary interface between applications and between applications and the system. We present a systematic study of security enforcement comprising 120 evaluations (99 inter-component interface evaluations across five interface categories, 10 platform security-control evaluations, and 11 dedicated positive controls) in over 30 Google and AOSP packages on Android 17 (API 37). Using an expected-versus-observed framework under a zero-permission attacker model, we evaluate whether each boundary's enforcement mechanism functions as designed. We find 97 enforcement gaps (80.8%) and 23 enforcement holds (19.2%). From these observations, we derive a 14-category enforcement gap taxonomy organized across manifest, code, platform, and architectural layers. Within our purposively selected corpus, observed enforcement outcomes differ substantially across interface categories: evaluated Activities and BroadcastReceivers exhibit a 100% gap rate, while ContentProviders, which benefit from framework-provided defenses such as setStrict(), achieve a 27.6% holds rate. We find that all seven evaluated platform compatibility changes with security intent are either disabled or gated at a targetSdkVersion that none of the applications in our evaluated corpus targets. We document 18 custom URI scheme registrations handling sensitive data (authentication tokens, payment credentials, medical information) despite the known unverifiability of custom schemes (RFC 8252 Section 8.1). Our study includes 23 positive controls, calibration cases demonstrating that the evaluation procedure distinguishes functioning enforcement from observed enforcement failures.
